title: Low-dimensional nanomaterials for electrochemical biosensing of gastric cancer biomarkers in whole blood: Current trends and future Prospects.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: 1 Introduction In recent years, there has been a notable rise in the incidence of cancer [ 1 ], becoming a major global health issue that affects individuals, families, and society [ 2 , 3 ]. Predictions for 2024 indicate that there will be over 960,000 new cases of gastric cancer (GC) and nearly 660,000 deaths worldwide [ [3] ,  [4] ,  [5] ,  [6] ], making it the fifth most common cancer and the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths in global [ 5 , 7 ]. GC is closely related to daily diet [ 8 ], overweight [ 9 ], high salt intake [ 10 , 11 ], consumption of smoked foods, and alcohol use [ 8 ]. Based on these factors, there are also significant geographical different in the incidence of GC, with rates in East Asia and Eastern Europe being 15–20 times higher than those in the African continent [ 12 ]. Clinical data indicates that the five-year survival rate for GC patients who are diagnosed and treated in the early stages is higher than that of patients with advanced GC [ [13] ,  [14] ,  [15] ]. Therefore, the development of more efficient early cancer diagnostic methods tailored to specific regions and populations remains a major challenge, which would enhance cancer prevention efforts and improve patient survival rates [ 16 ]. Whole blood has been extensively utilized in health management and clinical diagnosis due to its diverse range of potential biomarkers [ [17] ,  [18] ,  [19] ]. These biomarkers [ [20] ,  [21] ,  [22] ] include proteins, nucleic acids [ 23 ], enzymes [ 24 ], exosomes [ 25 , 26 ], and specific cell types [ 27 ] and others. The practicality and ease of blood biopsies make it as the preferred approach for cost-effective and rapid clinical detection [ 17 ]. More importantly, obtaining tumor biomarkers from whole blood is generally minimally invasive and well-tolerated by patients. Nevertheless, the low concentration of cancer biomarkers in the blood and their non-specific expression makes it challenging to achieve sufficient specificity and sensitivity for early cancer screening and real-time monitoring [ 28 , 29 ]. The advent of biosensor technology has introduced promising advancements in the field of cancer diagnosis [ 30 ]. Biosensors are analytical instruments that employ biorecognition elements, including antibodies, nucleic acid aptamers, or enzymes, to selectively bind to target analytes [ [31] ,  [32] ,  [33] ,  [34] ]. These devices convert biological recognition events into measurable signals—such as electrical [ [35] ,  [36] ,  [37] ], optical [ 38 , 39 ], or other forms [ 40 ]. Notably, among these technologies, electrochemical-based biosensors have attracted considerable interest due to their highly sensitive and specific in detection of cancer biomarkers [ [41] ,  [42] ,  [43] ]. Compared to the diagnosis of GC primarily depends on conventional techniques like endoscopy (which includes direct observation and biopsy, considered the gold standard) [ 44 , 45 ], MS [ [46] ,  [47] ,  [48] ,  [49] ], imaging methods (such as, CT and MRI for evaluating tumor stage and metastasis) [ 50 , 51 ], electrochemical sensor technology presents several notable advantages. Firstly, the non-invasive detection mode eliminates the traumatic risks associated with endoscopic procedures and reduces potential exposure to ionizing radiation from imaging examinations [ 52 ]. Secondly, it enables the highly sensitive detection of trace-level (fmol/L concentration) tumor biomarkers, significantly improving the detection rate of early-stage GC [ [53] ,  [54] ,  [55] ]. Lastly, this technology provides high throughput, with a single sample analysis time of less than 30 min and a 60–80 % reduction in per-test costs, making it particularly suitable for large-scale population screening and postoperative monitoring scenarios [ 52 ]. Recent studies have demonstrated that integrating low-dimensional nanomaterials as functional interface modification materials into electrochemical biosensors can significantly enhance their analytical performance [ 56 , 57 ]. First, the high specific surface area of low-dimensional materials, like graphene which has a theoretical value of 2630 m 2 /g, provides large number of active sites for the attachment of biomolecular recognition elements [ 58 ]. Second, the unique electronic structure significantly enhances the electrocatalytic current response by reducing energy barrier for electron transfer, leading to a significantly amplified faradaic current response [ 59 ]. Finally, the nanoscale confinement effect enables the detection limit to reach the attomolar level (10 −18  M), increasing the sensitivity by several orders of magnitude compared to traditional sensors [ [60] ,  [61] ,  [62] ]. In this review, we examined the recent advancements in electrochemical biosensors for the detection of GC in whole blood samples. We elucidating their basic operational principles, emphasizing the pivotal role of low-dimensional nanomaterials, which enhance the availability of binding sites for target molecules and enhance electron transfer efficiency. Furthermore, we address two critical research challenges: enhancing signal strength and ensuring specificity, where the unique physicochemical properties of low-dimensional nanomaterials play a pivotal role. Consequently, this review highlights the importance of structural engineering of low-dimensional nanomaterials for the construction of highly sensitive and selective electrochemical sensors for GC biomarkers. Finally, we evaluate the main challenges facing electrochemical-based GC biosensor and propose potential avenues for their development toward clinical application.

sections.heading: Principles of electrochemical measurements
sections.text: 2 Principles of electrochemical measurements Electrochemical measurement techniques are fundamental for obtaining critical data related to substance concentration, reaction kinetics, corrosion properties, and various other phenomena [ 61 ]. Notable electrochemical measurement techniques include amperometry, potentiometry, chronoamperometry, voltammetry, and impedance spectroscopy, among others [ 63 ]. 2.1 Amperometry In electrochemistry system, reactions produce measurable currents or change the electrical conductivity of the electrode interface. In chronoamperometry, a potential step is applied to the working electrode in a solution where mass transfer only occurs via diffusion. This yields a current-time profile that reflects changes in the concentration gradient near the electrode surface. 2.2 Potentiometry In potentiometric analysis, work electrode and reference electrode are place in the solution for measurement, forming an electrochemical cell. The potential difference measured between the electrodes is dependent on the electrochemical potential of the solution, which is influenced by the chemical properties of the components present. This change of potential can be used to determine the concentration or activity of the analyte in the solution, thereby providing valuable information regarding its chemical properties. 2.3 Voltammetry Voltammetry is highly regarded for its simplicity, remarkable sensitivity, and suitability for trace analysis, making it a widely used technique for both qualitative and quantitative evaluations of metal ions, organic compounds, and biologically active substances. Voltammetry methods include cyclic voltammetry (CV), linear sweep voltammetry (LSV), differential pulse voltammetry (DPV), and square wave voltammetry (SWV). Among these techniques, CV is the most frequently utilized for obtaining qualitative information about electrochemical reactions. It effectively provides thermodynamic data related to redox reactions, kinetic insights concerning heterogeneous electron transfer processes, coupling reflections, and comprehensive information on adsorption phenomena. LSV works by establishing a linear variation in time of the electrode potential between the working electrode and the reference electrode while recording the current through both the working and reference electrodes. LSV is used to examine a range of potential reactions and to assess the reversibility of electrode processes. DPV, introduced by Barker and Jenkin (1952), was developed to reduce the detection limits in voltammetric analysis by increasing the ratio of Faradaic to non-Faradaic currents. This technique effectively mitigates the background noise produced by the redox currents of impurities through the process of differential current subtraction. The SWV technique is defined as a differential method wherein the potential waveform applied to the working electrode consists of a symmetrical square wave superimposed on a base step potential. The peak voltammogram is symmetric with a half-wave potential, and its peak current is directly proportional to the concentration of the reactant. This method exhibits high sensitivity due to the net current being more pronounced than either the forward or reverse peak currents. 2.4 Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) EIS is defined as the total resistance that a device or circuit exhibits to the flow of alternating current (AC) at a specific frequency. This resistance is represented as a complex quantity and is depicted on a vector plane. The impedance vector consists of a real component, termed resistance (R), and an imaginary component, known as reactance (X). The evaluation of impedance provides dynamic and chemical information, aiding in the understanding of the electrochemical characteristics of different materials. EIS is recognized as a highly sensitive, cost-effective, label-free, and non-invasive technique for monitoring biological processes. 2.5 Photoelectrochemical (PEC) PEC biosensors are an innovative analytical methodology that integrates the PEC process with specific biorecognition mechanisms. In this method, PEC materials are activated by the light source, producing a photocurrent that serves as the detection signal. PEC biosensors significantly reduce background noise due to the complete separation of the incident light source from the detection signal. 2.6 Electrochemiluminescence (ECL) ECL refers to a phenomenon in which specific homogeneous electron transfer reactions produce chemiluminescence. This process generally involves three key components: the luminescent species, the co-reactant, and the electrode. When a voltage is added, a reaction occurs at the electrode, exciting the luminescent species to a higher energy state. As the species returns to its ground state, it emits a photon, resulting in the production of light. The ECL sensing technique utilizes the correlation between the emitted signal and the concentration of the target analyte, enabling precise detection of the analyte in a sample.
